layers.direct_answer: Young's modulus E measures tensile/compressive stiffness; in uniaxial linear elasticity, E = σ/ε, so σ = Eε.
layers.concept_expansion: E is the slope of the stress–strain curve in its linear elastic region. Because strain is dimensionless, E has the same units as stress, usually Pa or GPa.
layers.worked_or_physical_example: Steel has a much larger E than polystyrene, so under the same elastic stress steel strains much less.
layers.boundaries_and_misconceptions: Young's modulus measures stiffness, not strength. High E does not imply high yield or fracture strength.
layers.connections_and_memory: Steeper initial stress–strain slope → larger E → less elastic strain for a given stress.
layers.transfer_prompt: Two equal-geometry bars experience the same elastic stress. If one material has twice E, compare their strains.
layers.mastery_evidence: Define E, identify it from a stress–strain curve, state its units, and use it to compare elastic deformation.

cards.title: Stiffness vs Strength
cards.front: How are stiffness and strength different?

layers.direct_answer: Stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation; strength is the stress a material can withstand before a specified failure such as yielding or fracture.
layers.concept_expansion: Young's modulus quantifies elastic stiffness, while yield and ultimate strengths describe stress limits. They are distinct material properties.
layers.worked_or_physical_example: A material can have a steep elastic slope but fail at a comparatively low stress, while another can be less stiff yet survive higher stress.
layers.boundaries_and_misconceptions: A stronger material is not automatically stiffer, and a high Young's modulus does not tell you its yield strength.
layers.connections_and_memory: Stiffness asks 'how much will it deform?'; strength asks 'how much stress can it survive?'.
layers.transfer_prompt: A design already has ample failure margin but must deflect less. Which property should you prioritize?
layers.mastery_evidence: Choose correctly between modulus and strength for deformation-limited versus failure-limited design requirements.

cards.title: Atomic Origin of Young's Modulus
cards.front: What controls Young's modulus at the atomic scale?

layers.direct_answer: Young's modulus is governed primarily by how strongly interatomic bonds resist small changes in atomic spacing.
layers.concept_expansion: Near equilibrium spacing, stretching or compressing bonds requires force. The local stiffness of the interatomic potential appears macroscopically as elastic modulus.
layers.worked_or_physical_example: Materials whose bonds resist small spacing changes strongly generally require more stress to produce the same small elastic strain.
layers.boundaries_and_misconceptions: Young's modulus is a material property, not a specimen-geometry property. Geometry affects structural stiffness, which is different.
layers.connections_and_memory: Atomic bond stiffness → material modulus E → component deformation together with loading and geometry.
layers.transfer_prompt: Why can two same-sized bars have different elastic elongations under the same force even before either yields?
layers.mastery_evidence: Connect microscopic bond response to macroscopic elastic stiffness and distinguish material modulus from structural stiffness.
